newsitem.title: USA: TWA workers, friends gather for memorial.
newsitem.headline: TWA workers, friends gather for memorial.

text.p: Employees of TWA held a memorial service on Wednesday to honour their coworkers who died in the crash of Flight 800, the first of many services planned this week to mark the first anniversary of the tragedy.
Almost 1,000 TWA workers, many clad in pilots' uniforms, flight attendants' uniforms or mechanics' work clothes, attended the service in a hangar at New York's Kennedy International Airport.

Fifty-three TWA employees and family members were among the 230 people who died on board the Paris-bound jet. The Boeing 747 exploded in mid-air 11 minutes after taking off from Kennedy on July 17, 1996.
The cause of the crash has not been determined, although investigators suspect mechanical failure.
The service featured a poignant bagpipe, a choir, prayers and songs that echoed through the cavernous hangar.
A number of readers, some with their voices breaking, slowly intoned the names of the dead. Many in the audience held hands and cried.
"It makes me proud of being TWA," Joseph Bouadana, a TWA service manager and a 33-year employee, said afterward.
"I knew just about everybody working on the plane," he said. "And not a day goes by when you go on a flight that something pops up and reminds you of them."
The passing of a year since the crash has not made the loss any easier, said Ruth Callas, whose son Daniel was a flight attendant on the doomed jumbo jet.
"It's getting worse day after day," she said, through tears, after the service.

A highlight of the TWA service was the unveiling of a memorial to the victims of Flight 800. The six-foot-high statue features three etched glass panels showing the plane taking off, being cupped gently in a pair of hands and then being transformed into a bird.
"In my eyes, they're God's hands," said flight attendant Janet Collett, who submitted the winning design for the memorial. Her friend Warren Dodge was one of the TWA employees who died.
"I felt God is saying, 'These employees are safe there. They're at peace. Now it's time for you, your friends and your fellow employees to be at peace also.'"
Relatives of TWA victims were arriving in New York for a string of memorial services over the next few days.

"It's an extremely painful moment. At the same time it's a way to pay tribute to the 230 victims of Flight 800," said Michelle Richter in Paris as she prepared to board her New York-bound flight. She lost two teenage daughters in the crash.
Lead National Transportation Safety Board investigator Robert Francis said he and FBI assistant director James Kallstrom would be meeting families of the victims in the coming days.
"We will be spending as much time with them and giving them as much information as we can," Francis said in an interview with Reuters.
Kallstrom said he felt "sadness and emotion about the tragedy, the unfulfilled lives." He said the affects of the catastrophe had galvanised investigators to find the cause.
Investigators know that an explosion in the plane's near-empty centre fuel tank caused it to disintegrate, but they have not determined why.

Memorial services are scheduled for Thursday morning at St. Patrick's Cathedral in New York City and Thursday afternoon at Smith Point's Park in Long Island, a beach a few miles from where the plane went down.

Services also are planned on Friday at a cemetery and at a park in nearby Centre Moriches, New York. On Sunday, a service is scheduled to be held at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine in New York City.
